about: Cartagena's walled Old City, Getsemaní and the beachfront towers of Bocagrande and Castillogrande are what draw most foreign buyers, many of them planning a second home or a short-term rental. Colombian law treats foreign capital the same as local investment, and real estate is explicitly listed as a form of foreign investment. To keep the right to send the sale proceeds back abroad, bring the purchase money in through the formal foreign-exchange market: the exchange declaration doubles as the registration with the Banco de la República, and since Decreto 1044 of August 2026 investors can file any further registration declaration at any time rather than within a fixed deadline.

Title works through a public deed (escritura pública) signed before a notary and then entered on the property's folio de matrícula inmobiliaria at the Oficina de Registro de Instrumentos Públicos. Registration, not the deed alone, transfers ownership, and the registry's certificado de tradición y libertad shows the chain of owners, mortgages and liens, so ask your own lawyer to review it before paying a deposit. Colonial houses in the historic centre are protected heritage: any works need Ministry of Culture authorization that no ordinary building licence can replace, and a new protection plan (PEMP) approved in June 2026 was still awaiting its ministerial resolution in September 2026.

Weigh the risks honestly. The US State Department rates Colombia Level 3, 'Reconsider travel', and warns of drugging and armed break-ins where tourists stay, although its Level 4 areas do not include Bolívar. Waves have flooded streets in Castillogrande, and coastal-defence works along the seafront were still under way in July 2026. Short-term rental rules are tightening: every unit needs a free National Tourism Registry (RNT) listing, the building's rules must expressly allow tourist use, and national and district draft decrees in 2026 would add more conditions. Gross yields are among Colombia's lowest, about 5.2% against a national average near 7%, so do not buy on optimistic Airbnb projections.

faq.q: Can foreigners buy property in Cartagena, Colombia?
faq.a: Yes. Colombian law treats foreign investment the same as local investment, and real estate is a recognized form of foreign investment. Bring the money in through the formal exchange market so your investment is registered with the Banco de la República, which is what gives you the right to send the sale proceeds back abroad.

faq.q: Can I rent my Cartagena apartment on Airbnb?
faq.a: Only if the building allows it and you register. The Ministry of Commerce says the building's rules (reglamento de propiedad horizontal) must expressly allow tourist housing, and each host must hold a free National Tourism Registry (RNT) listing. New national and Cartagena draft decrees in 2026 could add further requirements, so check the current rules before you buy for rental income.

faq.q: How do I check the title of a property in Cartagena?
faq.a: Ask for the certificado de tradición y libertad from the Oficina de Registro de Instrumentos Públicos. It shows the registered owners, mortgages and liens on the property's folio de matrícula inmobiliaria. Ownership only passes when the deed is registered there.

faq.q: What does it cost to buy in Cartagena besides the price?
faq.a: Expect a departmental registration tax of 0.5% to 1% of the value, registry fees of roughly 0.9% to 1.3% on the 2026 sliding scale, and notary fees. The seller has 1% withheld at the notary as an advance on income tax.

cities.metaDescription: Buenos Aires real estate 2026: Zonaprop prices per m² by barrio, ~5.7% gross yields, foreign buyer rules, the CUIT, FX controls and the rent-law repeal.
about: Buenos Aires draws foreign buyers with its Belle Époque apartments in Recoleta and Palermo and prices that are modest for a capital of its size. Zonaprop's September 2026 index puts the average asking price of a city apartment at US$2,484/m², from about US$1,071 in Lugano to US$6,165 in Puerto Madero (Palermo US$3,454), with a gross rental yield of 5.70% for the city as a whole: 4.6% in Palermo and 3.2% in Puerto Madero, rising to 9.6% in Lugano. Those yields are asking rent over asking price, before vacancy, expenses (building fees), taxes and currency moves. Article 20 of the Constitution gives foreigners all the civil rights of citizens, including to buy and sell real estate, and no residency is required. The rural land law (Law 26.737), whose caps on foreign ownership were repealed by DNU 70/2023 and are back in the courts after the Supreme Court provisionally suspended that repeal in October 2026, applies only to land outside the urban ejido, so it does not affect city apartments.

A purchase must be made by escritura pública (Civil and Commercial Code, Art. 1017), signed before an escribano (notary) who may not authorise it without seeing the registered title and a current certificate from the Registro de la Propiedad Inmueble (Law 17.801, Art. 23); the deed is then registered there to be enforceable against third parties. A foreign buyer first needs an Argentine tax ID: since 2 March 2026, ARCA Resolución General 5803/2025 has replaced the old CDI with a CUIT, which non-residents request through a representative with an address in Argentina. In the city, stamp duty on the transfer is 2.7% when the price or fiscal value is up to ARS 226.1 million and 3.5% above that (Ley Tarifaria 2026, Art. 34). Listings are priced in US dollars, so agree with the escribano in advance how the funds will be transferred and documented.

Be clear about the risks. Argentina has a long history of currency controls (the 'cepo'). From 14 April 2025, BCRA Comunicación A 8226 let resident individuals buy dollars at banks for savings without prior central-bank approval, but that change covered resident individuals only, so confirm with your bank how a non-resident would take sale proceeds out. Rental rules were deregulated: DNU 70/2023 repealed the 2020 Rent Law (Law 27.551) and lets landlord and tenant set the term, currency and indexation. The Senate has rejected that decree and the Chamber of Deputies had not voted on it as of October 2026, so the rules could change again. Liquidity is real but mortgage-light: the city's notaries recorded 6,055 sale deeds in August 2026 (down 4.9% year on year), of which 1,059 used a mortgage (down 20.8%). The US State Department rates Argentina Level 1, 'Exercise normal precautions' (July 2026), while warning of petty crime in Buenos Aires.

faq.q: Can foreigners buy an apartment in Buenos Aires?
faq.a: Yes. Article 20 of the Argentine Constitution gives foreigners the same civil rights as citizens, including to buy and sell real estate, and no residency is needed. The rural land law limits foreign ownership only of land outside urban areas, so they do not apply to a city apartment.

faq.q: What tax ID does a foreigner need to buy property in Argentina?
faq.a: A CUIT. Since 2 March 2026, ARCA Resolución General 5803/2025 has replaced the CDI that foreigners used to obtain. Non-residents apply through a representative or authorised third party with an address in Argentina, using form 460 F/PD and a passport. CDIs issued before then remain valid until your details change.

faq.q: How much does an apartment cost in Buenos Aires in 2026?
faq.a: Zonaprop's September 2026 index puts the average asking price of a city apartment at US$2,484/m², from about US$1,071 in Lugano to US$6,165 in Puerto Madero; Palermo averages US$3,454. A typical 50 m² two-room flat is listed at about US$131,000. These are asking prices, and closing prices can be lower.

faq.q: Are Argentina's currency controls gone?
faq.a: Mostly, for residents. From 14 April 2025, BCRA Comunicación A 8226 let resident individuals buy foreign currency at banks without prior central-bank approval. The change applied to resident individuals, so non-residents should confirm with their bank how they would take sale proceeds or rent out of the country.

cities.metaDescription: Tulum, Mexico real estate 2026: bank trust rules for foreign buyers, ejido and permit risks, condo oversupply, asking prices and the US travel advisory.
about: Tulum, on Mexico's Caribbean coast in Quintana Roo, draws foreign buyers with its beaches and Maya ruins, its vacation-rental market, and better access: the Felipe Carrillo Puerto International Airport opened on 1 December 2023 and the town has a station on section 5 of the Tren Maya. Because Tulum lies inside Mexico's restricted zone (the strip within 50 km of the coast and 100 km of the borders), foreigners cannot hold residential title directly. Instead, a Mexican bank holds the title in a fideicomiso (bank trust) with the buyer as beneficiary. This needs a permit from the Secretaría de Relaciones Exteriores (SRE) and runs for up to 50 years, renewable on request. A Mexican company with foreign shareholders can own restricted-zone land directly, but only for non-residential use, and it must notify the SRE within 60 business days.

Title and permits are where Tulum deals go wrong. Ejido (communal) parcels can legally be sold only to other ejido members or recognized residents (avecindados) of the same ejido community until the ejido assembly approves full ownership (dominio pleno), the land is removed from the Registro Agrario Nacional and a private title is entered in the Public Property Registry. Environmental rules matter too. In 2022 the federal government decreed the 2,249-hectare Jaguar flora and fauna protection area in the municipality, where no new population centers are allowed, and the federal environmental agency Profepa has shut down developments in the municipality, including a hotel inside Tulum National Park (2018), and in September 2025 obtained a court-ordered seizure of the Adamar condo project at Tankah IV, built without federal environmental authorization. Bloomberg reported in 2025, citing lawyers, that more than 70 presale units in Tulum were never delivered, in some cases by developers that did not own the land.

The market risks are just as real. Expansión reported in July 2025 that new-home sales had fallen 32–35% since 2023, that vacation-rental occupancy averaged below 50% and that nightly rates kept falling, and AirDNA puts average occupancy at about 46% for the year to August 2026. With thousands of competing units, resale can be slow and rental income can fall short of developers' projections. The US State Department rates Quintana Roo, including Tulum, Level 2 ('Exercise increased caution') for terrorism and crime, and advises extra care after dark in downtown Tulum.

faq.q: Can foreigners buy property in Tulum?
faq.a: Yes, but not in their own name. Tulum is inside the restricted zone within 50 km of the coast, so a foreigner buying a home does so through a fideicomiso: a Mexican bank holds the title and the buyer is the beneficiary. The trust needs an SRE permit and lasts up to 50 years, renewable. A Mexican company can own land directly only for non-residential use.

faq.q: What is ejido land and why does it matter in Tulum?
faq.a: Ejido land is communally held agrarian land. Under the Ley Agraria, ejido parcels can be sold only to other ejido members or recognized residents (avecindados) of the same ejido community until the assembly approves full ownership and the land gets a private title registered in the Public Property Registry. Have your own lawyer confirm the private title and federal environmental permits before paying any deposit, including on a presale.

faq.q: Is Tulum oversupplied with condos?
faq.a: Reporting points that way. Expansión reported in July 2025 that new-home sales had fallen 32–35% since 2023 and that vacation-rental occupancy averaged below 50%. AirDNA puts average short-term-rental occupancy at about 46% for the year to August 2026. Plan on vacancy, discounting and a slow resale rather than the yields in sales brochures.

faq.q: Is Tulum safe according to the US State Department?
faq.a: The State Department's Mexico advisory rates Quintana Roo, which includes Tulum, Level 2 ('Exercise increased caution') for terrorism and crime, and advises extra care after dark in downtown Cancún, Tulum and Playa del Carmen. Check the live advisory before you travel or buy.

about: Santiago draws foreign buyers for depth and predictability rather than bargains. New apartments across Gran Santiago averaged 83 UF per m² (about CLP 3.4 million) in the three months to July 2026, up 5.4% on a year earlier, according to TOCTOC data reported by CNN Chile; the eastern communes most foreigners look at cost more in the unsubsidised segment, at 103 UF in Providencia, 114 UF in Las Condes and 117 UF in Vitacura. Prices are quoted in UF, an inflation-indexed unit worth about CLP 41,200 in October 2026, so a dollar buyer carries both peso and inflation-indexation exposure. Global Property Guide puts Santiago's average gross apartment yield at 4.91% in Q1 2026 and notes net yields typically run 1.5 to 2 points lower.

Chile's trade-agreement reservations list only narrow restrictions on foreign ownership of real estate: state land within 10 km of the border or 5 km of the coast is reserved for Chileans unless a legal exception applies, and in declared border zones nationals of neighboring countries, and companies based in or controlled by them, need a presidential exemption. Owners pay an annual property tax (contribuciones), which the SII charges on the fiscal appraisal: from July 2026 the first CLP 61,711,570 of a home's appraisal is exempt, the rest pays 0.893%, and value above CLP 220,398,431 pays 1.042%.

The honest risks are currency and timing. Supply is tightening (the Santiago region had 49,834 new apartments for sale at the end of July 2026, 18.2% fewer than a year earlier), but much of the pipeline story depends on infrastructure that is still years away: Metro Line 7, 26 km and 19 stations from Renca to Vitacura, was about 40% complete in early 2026 and is expected to open at the end of 2028. The US State Department rates Chile Level 2, 'Exercise increased caution', citing crime, including violent crime such as carjackings in Santiago, and demonstrations that can disrupt buses and the metro.

faq.q: Can foreigners buy property in Santiago, Chile?
faq.a: Chile's trade-agreement reservations list only narrow restrictions on foreign ownership: state land within 10 km of the border or 5 km of the coast is reserved for Chileans unless a legal exception applies, and in declared border zones buyers from neighboring countries need a presidential exemption. Have your lawyer confirm that no restriction applies to the specific property.

faq.q: How much does an apartment cost in Santiago in 2026?
faq.a: New apartments in Gran Santiago averaged 83 UF per m² (about CLP 3.4 million) in the three months to July 2026, according to TOCTOC. In the unsubsidised segment, Providencia averaged 103 UF, Las Condes 114 UF and Vitacura 117 UF per m².

faq.q: What is the property tax on a home in Santiago?
faq.a: Contribuciones are charged by the SII on the fiscal appraisal, not the price. From July 2026 the first CLP 61,711,570 of a home's appraisal is exempt; the rest pays 0.893%, and any value above CLP 220,398,431 pays 1.042%. They are paid in four installments in April, June, September and November.

faq.q: What rental yield can I expect in Santiago?
faq.a: Global Property Guide puts the average gross yield on Santiago apartments at 4.91% in Q1 2026, with yields ranging from 3.84% to 5.85% depending on unit size. Net yields are typically 1.5 to 2 percentage points lower.

cities.metaDescription: Montevideo, Uruguay real estate 2026: equal rights for foreigners, ~$2,840/m² median asking, 5–6% gross yields, closing costs and the new-resident tax holiday.
about: Montevideo draws foreign buyers with a legal system that treats them like locals and a market priced in US dollars. Uruguay's investment law (Law 16.906) gives foreign investors the same treatment as nationals, and anyone, national or foreign, can own real estate. In the Índice INGAR for September 2026, the median asking price for apartments across Montevideo's barrios was about $2,840/m², rising to $3,956 in Pocitos, $4,184 in Punta Carretas and $4,370 in Carrasco. Estimated gross yields ran about 5–5.5% in those prime areas and 6.2% in Cordón and Centro. Since January 1, 2026, people who become tax residents can choose to pay non-resident income tax (IRNR) instead of IRPF on foreign investment income for the year they arrive plus the next ten. That applies if they spend more than 183 days a year in Uruguay or meet an investment test, such as more than UI 12.5 million in real estate, and were not tax residents in the previous two years.

The purchase runs through an escribano público, a notary chosen by the buyer. The escribano studies the title, drafts the escritura (deed), withholds the taxes and registers the first copy of the deed at the Registro de la Propiedad, Sección Inmobiliaria. That registry is run by the Dirección General de Registros and organised by the department where the property sits. Typical buyer costs are a notary fee of about 3% plus 22% VAT, an agent's commission of 3% plus VAT if an agent is involved, and the 2% property transfer tax (ITP). The seller pays another 2% ITP. ITP is charged on the cadastral value, which is usually well below the market price, so one Montevideo law firm estimates total buyer costs at 5–9% of the price.

The main risks are crime, cost and thin data. The US State Department rates Uruguay Level 2, 'Exercise increased caution', because of crime, in an advisory issued July 28, 2026. It says homicide, armed robbery, carjacking and theft are most common in Montevideo, Canelones, Maldonado and Rivera. Price and yield figures come from asking prices, not closed sales, and gross yields fall once tax, vacancy, management and building fees are counted. Montevideo is also expensive for the region: Numbeo puts a single person's monthly costs at about $970 before rent.

faq.q: Can foreigners buy property in Montevideo, Uruguay?
faq.a: Yes, on the same terms as Uruguayans. Law 16.906 gives foreign investors the same treatment as nationals, and anyone, national or foreign, can own and occupy real estate.

faq.q: What are the closing costs when buying in Montevideo?
faq.a: Buyers typically pay a notary fee of about 3% plus 22% VAT, an agent's commission of 3% plus VAT if an agent is involved, and 2% property transfer tax (ITP) on the cadastral value, plus small title-study and registration fees. One Montevideo law firm puts the total at 5–9% of the price.

faq.q: Does Uruguay still have a 10-year tax holiday for new residents?
faq.a: In a changed form. For people who become tax residents from January 1, 2026, Law 20.446 lets them pay non-resident income tax (IRNR) instead of IRPF on foreign investment income for the year they become resident plus ten more. To qualify they must spend more than 183 days a year in Uruguay or invest more than UI 12.5 million in real estate or at least UI 625,000 a year in qualifying funds, and must not have been tax residents in the previous two years. Confirm your case with a Uruguayan tax adviser.

faq.q: Is Montevideo safe for foreign property buyers?
faq.a: The US State Department rates Uruguay Level 2, 'Exercise increased caution', because of crime, in its July 28, 2026 advisory. It names Montevideo among the departments where crime is most common, with homicide, armed robbery, carjacking and theft the main concerns.

cities.metaDescription: Punta del Este, Uruguay real estate 2026: median asking price per m², 2% ITP transfer tax, 12% gains tax, foreign buyer rules and seasonal rental risk.
about: Punta del Este, on Uruguay's Maldonado coast, draws most of its buyers from across the River Plate: Argentines still make up the majority, followed by Uruguayans, and Brazilian investors are a growing group, according to El Observador. Demand runs from the peninsula, which agents say is gaining relevance, along Playa Brava (the area premium buyers prefer), Playa Mansa and Roosevelt, out to La Barra, traditionally favoured by Argentines; in José Ignacio, apartment development is still in its early stages. Property is priced and sold in US dollars. An index of listings from late September 2026 put the median asking price at about US$3,909 per m² for resale apartments and US$4,091 for new ones, as reported by El Observador. These are asking prices, not closing prices.

Foreigners buy on the same terms as Uruguayans: Law 16.906 gives foreign investors the same treatment as nationals. An escribano (notary) handles the deed, and the purchase is recorded at the Registro de la Propiedad, Sección Inmobiliaria, run by the Dirección General de Registros. At purchase, the buyer and the seller each pay 2% transfer tax (ITP), charged on the valor real set by the Dirección Nacional de Catastro rather than on the price, according to the DGI. Owners then pay the annual Contribución Inmobiliaria to the Intendencia de Maldonado plus the national Primaria tax of 1.5 to 3 per thousand of valor real, and individuals may owe wealth tax (Impuesto al Patrimonio) on Uruguayan assets above a tax-free minimum of about US$166,000, at progressive rates up to 1.5%, according to Uruguay XXI.

Expect a seasonal market built around the summer: for the 2024–25 season El Observador reported very high January booking levels, with the challenge being to hold demand into February and March. Because Argentines are the largest buyer group, Argentina's economy and exchange rate move both rentals and sales, and dollar pricing adds currency risk for anyone earning in pesos or reais. When you sell, the DGI taxes the gain at 12%, withheld by the escribano (for property bought before July 1, 2007 the seller can instead be taxed on 15% of the price or Catastro value, whichever is higher); non-residents pay IRNR, generally at 12%. Under Law 20.446, people who become tax residents from January 1, 2026 can opt out of IRPF on foreign investment income for their first year and the ten following; one route is holding more than UI 12.5 million in Uruguayan real estate, and they must not have been tax residents in the previous two years. We have not found a reliable published rental yield for Punta del Este, so model rental income conservatively.

faq.q: Can foreigners buy property in Punta del Este?
faq.a: Yes. Uruguay's investment law (Law 16.906) gives foreign investors the same treatment as nationals, so you can buy in your own name without residency. An escribano (notary) handles the deed, and the purchase is recorded at the Registro de la Propiedad, Sección Inmobiliaria.

faq.q: What taxes do I pay when buying and owning in Punta del Este?
faq.a: At purchase, the buyer and the seller each pay 2% ITP on the valor real set by the Dirección Nacional de Catastro, not on the price. Each year you pay the Contribución Inmobiliaria to the Intendencia de Maldonado and the national Primaria tax (1.5 to 3 per thousand of valor real). Individuals may also owe wealth tax (Impuesto al Patrimonio) on Uruguayan assets above a tax-free minimum of about US$166,000.

faq.q: Is there capital gains tax when I sell property in Punta del Este?
faq.a: Yes. The DGI taxes the gain on selling urban property at 12%, withheld by the escribano at the sale, and non-residents pay the equivalent IRNR, generally at 12%. For property bought before July 1, 2007, the seller can instead be taxed on 15% of the price or Catastro value, whichever is higher.

faq.q: How much does an apartment cost per square metre in Punta del Este?
faq.a: An index of listings from late September 2026 put the median asking price at about US$3,909 per m² for resale apartments and US$4,091 for new ones, as reported by El Observador. These are asking prices, not sale prices, and they exclude Pinares and Maldonado city.

cities.metaDescription: Lima, Peru real estate 2026 — Miraflores, Barranco, San Isidro prices, rental yields, foreign ownership rules and cost of living.
about: Lima is a metropolitan area of about 10 million people, and most foreign buyers focus on the ocean-side districts of Miraflores, Barranco and San Isidro. Peru's Constitution (Article 71) puts foreigners on the same footing as Peruvians for property ownership, so you can buy in your own name with no residency, local partner or trust. The restriction applies only within 50 km of the country's borders, far from Lima. Central bank (BCRP) data put median asking prices in Q1 2026 at about US$2,460 per square meter in Miraflores, US$2,560 in Barranco and US$2,600 in San Isidro, and dollar prices rose about 10–21% over the previous year.

Ownership is transferred by a public deed (escritura pública) signed before a notary and then registered with SUNARP, the public registry. SUNARP stresses that the deed alone is not enough: register the sale, check the registry certificate before you buy, and ask the notary for a registry block until signing. The buyer pays the 3% alcabala transfer tax on the value above 10 UIT (S/ 55,000 in 2026). A non-resident individual landlord pays a 5% tax on gross rent, which a domiciled tenant withholds.

The risks are real. The US State Department rates Peru Level 2, 'Exercise increased caution', citing crime, unrest, kidnapping and terrorism, and Lima and Callao have been under repeated states of emergency since September 2024 over killings and extortion. Lima sits in a major earthquake zone, and the civil defence agency INDECI warns of a possible magnitude 8.8 quake off the central coast, so check a building's age and its compliance with the E.030 seismic code. Politics are volatile: Keiko Fujimori's July 2026 inauguration was Peru's ninth change of president in ten years. Gross yields are moderate, at about 5.5–6%, and published prices are asking prices, so budget time and negotiating room for resale.

faq.q: Can foreigners buy property in Lima, Peru?
faq.a: Yes. Article 71 of Peru's Constitution gives foreigners the same property rights as Peruvians, so you can buy an apartment in Lima in your own name with no residency or local partner. The only restriction is within 50 km of the borders, which does not affect Lima.

faq.q: How much does an apartment cost per square meter in Miraflores?
faq.a: BCRP data put the median asking price at about US$2,460 per square meter in Miraflores in Q1 2026, with San Isidro at about US$2,600 and Barranco about US$2,560. Urbania's July 2026 index had Miraflores at S/ 8,905 per square meter.

faq.q: What rental yield can I expect in Lima?
faq.a: About 5.5–6% gross. BCRP price-to-rent ratios for Q1 2026 imply about 5.6% in Miraflores and 6.0% in San Isidro, and Urbania put Lima's average at 5.53% in July 2026. Non-resident landlords pay a 5% tax on gross rent.

faq.q: What taxes do I pay when buying property in Lima?
faq.a: The buyer pays the alcabala transfer tax: 3% of the value above 10 UIT, or above S/ 55,000 in 2026. In the province of Lima it is paid to SAT Lima by the last business day of the month after the transfer.

cities.metaDescription: São Paulo real estate 2026 for foreigners: R$12,206/m² asking prices, 6.4% gross yields, CPF, deed and registry steps, 3% ITBI, taxes and honest risks.
about: São Paulo draws foreign buyers for its scale and its rents: FipeZAP's September 2026 index puts the average residential asking price at R$12,206 per m² (about US$2,420 at the Banco Central PTAX rate of R$5.04 per dollar) and the average gross rental yield at 6.43%, above Brazil's 6.13% average, with the highest average asking rent of the 22 capitals FipeZAP tracks, R$65.78 per m² a month. Foreigners can buy urban property here on the same terms as Brazilians; the federal limits on foreign ownership apply to rural land and the 150 km border strip, not to city apartments.

Buying runs through three steps. You first need a CPF taxpayer number, which non-residents can request free through the Receita Federal or a Brazilian consulate. For property worth more than 30 minimum wages the sale must be signed as an escritura pública before a notary (Civil Code Art. 108), and ownership only passes when that deed is registered on the property's matrícula at the Registro de Imóveis (Art. 1,245). The city charges ITBI transfer tax of 3% on the higher of the price and the city's reference value, according to the Prefeitura; ask your lawyer which base applies to your purchase. Investor residency is possible with at least R$1,000,000 in property under CNIg Normative Resolution 36/2018; confirm the current rules with the Ministry of Justice before relying on it.

Be realistic about returns and exit. Prices rose 3.64% in the twelve months to September 2026, below FipeZAP's 4.45% consumer-inflation measure, so they fell slightly in real terms, and FipeZAP notes that the national yield is below Brazil's real reference interest rate. Unsold new-build stock reached 98,018 units in August 2026, up 50.7% in a year, and the estimated time to sell mid- and high-end units has stretched to about 13 months. Since 2021 the dollar has traded between about R$4.62 and R$6.21 (Banco Central PTAX), and non-resident landlords pay 15% withholding tax on rent. Condo fees average roughly R$840–1,090 a month. The US State Department rates Brazil Level 2, 'Exercise Increased Caution', citing crime and kidnapping, with 'Do Not Travel' zones that include favelas and land border areas.

faq.q: Can foreigners buy property in São Paulo?
faq.a: Yes. Brazilian law restricts foreign ownership of rural land and land in the 150 km border strip, not urban apartments, so a foreigner can buy in São Paulo in their own name. You will need a CPF taxpayer number first, which non-residents can request free through the Receita Federal or a Brazilian consulate.

faq.q: What does an apartment cost per square metre in São Paulo?
faq.a: FipeZAP's September 2026 index puts the average residential asking price at R$12,206 per m², about US$2,420 at the Banco Central exchange rate of R$5.04 per dollar. Prices rose 3.64% over the previous twelve months.

faq.q: What rental yield can I expect in São Paulo?
faq.a: FipeZAP estimated the average gross rental yield at 6.43% a year in September 2026, against 6.13% for Brazil. That is before condo fees (roughly R$840–1,090 a month on average), IPTU property tax, vacancy and the 15% withholding tax non-resident landlords pay on rent.

faq.q: What taxes do foreigners pay when buying and selling in São Paulo?
faq.a: The city charges 3% ITBI transfer tax when you buy. When you sell, a non-resident's gain is calculated in reais and taxed at 15% up to R$5 million, rising in steps to 22.5%, so a fall in the real can leave you owing tax on a gain that is a loss in dollars.

cities.metaDescription: Florianópolis, Brazil real estate 2026: FipeZap prices near R$13,600/m², 5.4% gross yields, CPF, escritura, 2% ITBI and terreno de marinha rules for foreigners.
about: Florianópolis, the capital of Santa Catarina, is split between Santa Catarina Island and a mainland district, and had 537,211 residents in the 2022 Census. Foreign interest centres on the island's beach neighbourhoods, such as Jurerê, Canasvieiras, Ingleses and Armação, and on Lagoa da Conceição; the state government notes heavy summer tourism, much of it from Argentina. It is not cheap: in September 2026 the FipeZap index put the average residential asking price at R$13,607/m², up 8.3% in 12 months, the second highest of the state capitals it tracks after Vitória and well above the R$10,015/m² index average. FipeZap's gross long-term rental yield for the city was about 5.4% a year.

Foreigners can buy urban property in their own name; rural land is subject to a separate regime under Law 5.709/1971, which caps foreign holdings at a quarter of a municipality's area. You first need a CPF tax number, which non-residents request free of charge at a Brazilian consulate. Above 30 times the minimum wage, the Civil Code requires the sale to be made by escritura pública, signed at a tabelionato de notas, and ownership only passes when that deed is registered at the Cartório de Registro de Imóveis; until then the seller is still the legal owner. Florianópolis charges ITBI transfer tax at 2% under its tax code (art. 285-A), with 0.5% on the part financed through the SFH housing system up to an inflation-indexed cap.

Two local issues need a lawyer's check. Much of the shoreline is terreno de marinha: Union land within 33 m of the 1831 mean high-tide line, including around islands, managed by the SPU. Holders pay an annual fee (0.6% of land value for aforamento), and the seller pays the Union a 5% laudêmio on the land value when it is sold. A 2018 press report counted about 42,000 such plots in the city, 39,000 not yet finally demarcated. Federal law also protects mangroves, restingas and a 30 m strip around natural lakes in urban zones, and courts have blocked new building permits in protected areas such as Praia Brava. Prices are in reais, so returns move with the exchange rate, and there is no reliable published data on short-term rental returns.

faq.q: Can foreigners buy property in Florianópolis?
faq.a: Yes. Urban property can be bought in a foreigner's own name; rural land falls under Law 5.709/1971, which limits foreign ownership. You need a Brazilian CPF tax number, which non-residents get free at a Brazilian consulate, before you sign.

faq.q: What taxes do you pay when buying in Florianópolis?
faq.a: The municipality charges ITBI transfer tax at 2% (0.5% on the part financed through the SFH, up to a cap). If the property is on federal coastal land (terreno de marinha), the seller also pays the Union a 5% laudêmio on the land value, and the owner pays an annual fee to the SPU. Notary and registry fees come on top.

faq.q: What is a terreno de marinha and why does it matter?
faq.a: It is federal land within 33 m of the 1831 mean high-tide line, along the coast and around islands, managed by the SPU. You hold use rights rather than full ownership, pay an annual fee and owe laudêmio on resale. A 2018 press report counted about 42,000 such plots in Florianópolis, so ask your lawyer to check the SPU status of any coastal property.

faq.q: What rental yield can I expect in Florianópolis?
faq.a: FipeZap put the gross long-term rental yield at about 5.4% a year in September 2026, based on asking rents and prices, before taxes, vacancy and costs. There is no reliable published data for short-term holiday rental returns.

cities.metaDescription: Granada, Nicaragua real estate 2026: foreign buyer rules, title and confiscation risks, the 2025 constitution, thin price data and the US travel advisory.
about: Granada, on the shore of Lake Nicaragua, is one of Central America's oldest colonial cities, and its restored courtyard houses are what draw most foreign buyers. Foreigners can buy property here in their own name: The US State Department reports no specific restrictions on foreign or non-resident investors apart from border and national-security areas, and a standard purchase needs no residency permit, local partner or minimum investment. The 2025 constitution protects property in Article 40 but allows expropriation 'with fair compensation', and the same State Department report documents seizures of foreign-owned property. In August 2026 the government took nine homes owned by US retirees in Tola, Rivas; eight were returned in October.

The real work is the title. Purchases are signed as an escritura pública before a Nicaraguan notary and then entered in the Registro Público under Law 698 of 2009. The US Embassy estimates about 28,000 properties were confiscated between 1979 and 1990 and many remain disputed, and colonial houses tend to have the longest ownership chains, so a full title study by your own lawyer is essential before any deposit.

Buyers should also weigh the political backdrop. As of May 2026 the US State Department rates Nicaragua Level 3, 'Reconsider travel', citing crime, limited healthcare, wrongful detention and other risks. Granada's prices are low by regional standards, but liquidity is thinner than in Costa Rica or Panama, so plan for a longer hold and a slower resale.

faq.q: Can foreigners buy property in Granada, Nicaragua?
faq.a: Legally, yes. The US State Department reports no specific restrictions on foreign or non-resident buyers apart from border and national-security areas, including a 15 km strip along land borders declared state property in 2025. But the same report says the government has seized foreign-owned property, so treat any purchase as high-risk.

faq.q: What is the biggest risk when buying in Granada?
faq.a: Title history. The US Embassy estimates around 28,000 properties were confiscated between 1979 and 1990 and many are still disputed. Hire your own lawyer, order a full title study at the Registro Público, and never rely on an unregistered deed.

faq.q: Is it safe to buy property in Nicaragua right now?
faq.a: The US State Department rated Nicaragua Level 3, 'Reconsider travel', in its May 2026 advisory, citing crime, limited healthcare and the risk of wrongful detention. In August 2026 the government also took nine homes owned by US retirees in Tola, Rivas, so it is a much higher-risk market than Costa Rica or Panama.

faq.q: Can I get residency in Nicaragua as a retiree?
faq.a: Possibly, but the rules changed: the old pensionado law (Law 694) was repealed by the 2024 General Tourism Law (Law 1210), and retiree residency now falls under the general migration law. Confirm the current requirements and income threshold with the Dirección General de Migración y Extranjería or an immigration lawyer before applying.

cities.metaDescription: San Juan del Sur, Nicaragua real estate 2026: asking prices, coastal-zone law 690, title and confiscation risks, border-strip rules and the US travel advisory.
about: San Juan del Sur is a small Pacific bay town in Nicaragua's Rivas department, and its surf beaches and ocean-view hillsides are what draw most foreign buyers. Homes and condos are listed in US dollars: the middle half of 23 Encuentra24 listings with a stated built area asked about US$1,650–2,450 per square metre of built area in October 2026, from about US$850 for modest houses to about US$3,200 for some beachfront condos. Foreigners can hold title in their own name: the US State Department reports no specific restrictions on foreign buyers outside border and national-security areas, and the 2025 constitution protects property in Article 40 while allowing expropriation 'with fair compensation'; the same report documents seizures of foreign-owned property, and in August 2026 the government took nine homes owned by US retirees in nearby Tola.

Coastal land has its own rules. Under Ley 690 of 2009, the Coastal Zones Development Law, the beach between low and high tide plus 50 metres inland from the average high-tide mark is state-owned public-use land where homes are prohibited, and the next 200 metres inland is a restricted zone where the state regulates use. Neither strip can be sold, only granted by concession, although rights legally acquired before the law and already-established urban centres are exempt. Purchases are recorded in the Registro Público de la Propiedad, part of the national registry system set up by Law 698 of 2009. The US Embassy says about 28,000 properties were expropriated between 1979 and 1990, many are still disputed, and it urges extreme caution with coastal property in particular.

The country risk is real. The US State Department rates Nicaragua Level 3, 'Reconsider travel', citing crime, health, wrongful detention and arbitrary enforcement of local laws. In August 2025 the National Assembly passed Law 1258, which declares a 15-kilometre strip along Nicaragua's borders state property, and the State Department called it a 'massive confiscation'. The town itself is roughly 25–30 km from the Costa Rican border, outside the strip, but the municipality's southern beaches (El Ostional, La Flor, Playa El Coco) lie within or close to it, so have a lawyer confirm where any lot sits. Nicaragua publishes no sales-price data and no reliable rental-yield figures, so treat agents' yield claims with caution and plan for a long hold.

faq.q: Can foreigners buy beachfront property in San Juan del Sur?
faq.a: Foreigners can own private land in their own name, but not the beach itself. Ley 690 makes the area between the tides plus 50 metres inland from the average high-tide mark public-use state land where homes are banned, and the next 200 metres inland is a restricted zone. Rights legally acquired before 2009 are respected, so your lawyer must check exactly where any lot sits.

faq.q: How much does property cost in San Juan del Sur?
faq.a: There is no official price index. In a sample of 23 Encuentra24 listings with a stated built area (October 2026), the middle half asked about US$1,650–2,450 per square metre of built area, from about US$850 for modest houses to about US$3,200 for some beachfront condos. Treat these as asking prices, not sale prices.

faq.q: What are the biggest risks of buying in San Juan del Sur?
faq.a: Title and politics. The US Embassy says about 28,000 properties were expropriated in 1979-1990, many are still disputed, and it urges extreme caution with coastal property. Law 1258 of 2025 also made a 15 km strip along Nicaragua's borders state property: the town is outside it, but the southern beaches such as El Ostional, La Flor and Playa El Coco are within or close to it. Order a full title study at the Registro Público before paying any deposit.

faq.q: Is it safe to buy property in Nicaragua right now?
faq.a: The US State Department rates Nicaragua Level 3, 'Reconsider travel', citing crime, health, wrongful detention and arbitrary enforcement of local laws, and the US Embassy urges extreme caution when buying coastal property. Weigh that risk, and the slow resale market, before committing.
